claim: Klebsiella quasipneumoniae FK688 is carbapenem-resistant but carries no carbapenemase-encoding genes.
source: A combination of short- and long-read sequencing, machine learning, and genetic and enzymatic analyses established that this carbapenem-resistant strain carries no carbapenemase-encoding genes.
evidence: Supported by genome sequencing data, machine learning predictions using DeepBL, and enzymatic activity assays showing no carbapenemase activity

claim: Two distinct genetic loci are necessary for FK688 to acquire carbapenem resistance.
source: Genetic reconstruction of the resistance phenotype confirmed that two distinct genetic loci are necessary in order for the strain to acquire carbapenem resistance.
evidence: Confirmed through genetic reconstruction experiments and MIC testing

claim: Both loci required for carbapenem resistance confer a significant fitness cost and are readily lost in the absence of antibiotic selection.
source: Experimental evolution of the carbapenem-resistant strains in growth conditions without the antibiotic revealed that both loci confer a significant cost and are readily lost by de novo mutations resulting in the rapid evolution of a carbapenem-sensitive phenotype.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental evolution experiments showing loss of resistance genes and fitness assays

claim: Selection in ceftazidime can select for the blaDHA-1 gene, potentiating the evolution of carbapenem resistance by a single mutation in ompK36.
source: Fitness assays in a range of drug concentrations show how selection in the antibiotic ceftazidime can select for one gene ( bla DHA-1 ) potentiating the evolution of carbapenem resistance by a single mutation in a second gene ( ompK36 ).
evidence: Supported by fitness assays across different ceftazidime concentrations showing selective advantage of blaDHA-1

claim: A patient's treatment history might shape the evolution of antibiotic resistance.
source: These results show how a patient's treatment history might shape the evolution of antibiotic resistance and could explain the genetic basis of carbapenem-resistance found in many enteric-pathogens.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing sequential selection for resistance genes

claim: FK688 is classified as Klebsiella quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae.
source: Phylogenetic analysis placed FK688 within K. quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Determined through phylogenetic analysis of genome sequences

claim: FK688 carries a circular chromosome of 5,211,811 bp and a novel circular megaplasmid pNAR of 1,257,585 bp.
source: The genome assembly revealed a circular chromosome (5,211,811 bp) and a novel circular megaplasmid (pNAR; 1,257,585 bp).
evidence: Determined through complete genome assembly using long- and short-read sequencing

claim: The megaplasmid pNAR1 carries many antibiotic resistance genes corresponding to the known resistance profile of FK688.
source: This plasmid carried many antibiotic resistance genes corresponding to the known resistance profile (Bi et al., 2017), as well as genes encoding efflux pumps and other transporters (Figure 1—source data 3, Figure 1-source data 4).
evidence: Identified through genome annotation and comparison with known resistance profile

claim: FK688 chromosome contains blaOKP-B-21 gene encoding a β-lactamase that confers resistance to penicillins and cephalosporins such as cefazolin.
source: Readily identifiable determinants of AMR on the FK688 chromosome are a blaOKP-B-21 gene encoding a β-lactamase that confers resistance to penicillins and cephalosporins such as cefazolin
evidence: Identified through genome annotation

claim: FK688 chromosome contains determinants for quinolone resistance (oqxA, oqxB) and fosfomycin resistance (fosA5).
source: as well as determinants for quinolone (oqxA, oqxB; Brisse et al., 2014; Mathers et al., 2019; Rodrigues et al., 2019) and fosfomycin (fosA5) resistance
evidence: Identified through genome annotation and supported by literature citations

claim: FK688 does not encode the KPC-2 carbapenemase found in many K. quasipneumoniae isolates.
source: Our genome sequence analysis did not reveal a gene encoding KPC-2, the carbapenemase found in many K. quasipneumoniae isolates (Mathers et al., 2019).
evidence: Determined through genome sequence analysis

claim: DeepBL machine learning predictor generated eight high-confidence predictions for β-lactamases in FK688, with blaOKP-B-21 and blaDHA-1 being the two highest predictions.
source: DeepBL identifies genes encoding β-lactamases of all types, including carbapenemases, and generated eight high-confidence predictions. The two highest predictions represent known β-lactamases blaOKP-B-21 and blaDHA-1.
evidence: Generated using DeepBL machine learning tool on FK688 genome

claim: Only OKP-B-21 and DHA-1 have β-lactamase activity that includes significant resistance to ceftazidime among the eight DeepBL candidates tested.
source: Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) assays of E. coli expressing the DeepBL candidates showed that only OKP-B-21 and DHA-1 have β-lactamase activity that includes significant resistance to ceftazidime, a third-generation cephalosporin (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 6).
evidence: Demonstrated through MIC assays of E. coli expressing candidate genes

claim: Neither OKP-B-21 nor DHA-1, nor any of the other proteins tested, provided resistance to carbapenems.
source: However, neither OKP-B-21 nor DHA-1 - nor any of the other proteins tested - provided resistance to carbapenems.
evidence: Demonstrated through MIC assays testing carbapenem resistance

claim: The carbapenem-resistant phenotype for FK688 is not caused by a carbapenemase.
source: Taken together with the genome sequence analysis, these data support that the observed carbapenem-resistant phenotype for FK688 is not caused by a carbapenemase.
evidence: Concluded from genome analysis and enzymatic activity assays

claim: K. pneumoniae has four genes encoding the major porins OmpK35, OmpK36, OmpK37, and OmpK38.
source: K. pneumoniae has four genes encoding the major porins OmpK35, OmpK36, OmpK37, and OmpK38 (Rocker et al., 2020)
evidence: Established knowledge from cited literature

claim: The position and synteny of each porin gene in FK688 are conserved across K. quasipneumoniae.
source: and the position and synteny of each gene in FK688 are conserved across K. quasipneumoniae (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated through comparative genomic analysis

claim: FK688 has a 1.3 kb transposase gene (IS4 family) insertion within the 5' end of the ompK35 gene.
source: Inspection of the predicted protein sequences encoded by the four genes in FK688 revealed a 1.3 kb transposase gene (IS4 family) insertion within the 5' end of the ompK35 gene (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Identified through genome sequence analysis

claim: FK688 has a 48 bp in-frame deletion in ompK36.
source: and a 48 bp in-frame deletion in ompK36 in FK688 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Identified through genome sequence analysis

claim: The 48 bp deletion in ompK36 removes 16 amino acids at the 3' end of the gene, encompassing large portions of the β14 and β15 strands of the β-barrel structure.
source: The structure of OmpK36 (PDB 5O79) is known (Acosta-Gutiérrez et al., 2018), and the identified deletion of 16 amino acids at the 3' end of the ompK36 gene in FK688 encompasses large portions of the β14 and β15 strands of the β-barrel structure (Figure 2A and Figure 2B)
evidence: Determined by mapping deletion to known protein structure

claim: The deletion in ompK36 explains why the OmpK36 protein is not assembled into the outer membrane of FK688.
source: explaining why the protein is not assembled into the outer membrane of FK688.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis showing disruption of critical β-barrel strands

claim: Repair of the OmpK36 gene in FK688 restored carbapenem sensitivity.
source: Finally, measurements of carbapenem MIC determined that the repaired gene encoding the porin OmpK36 restored carbapenem sensitivity (Table 2).
evidence: Demonstrated through genetic complementation and MIC testing

claim: After 11 passages without β-lactam antibiotic selection, two out of 10 replicate FK688 lineages completely lost resistance to ceftazidime.
source: After 11 passages, two replicates had completely lost resistance to the β-lactam antibiotic ceftazidime.
evidence: Observed in mutation accumulation experiment

claim: One FK688 lineage lost a 17 kb region of pNAR1 that included the blaDHA-1 and qnrB4 antibiotic resistance genes flanked by tnpA-sul1 gene mobility elements.
source: The first lineage lost a 17 kb region of pNAR1 that included the blaDHA-1 and qnrB4 antibiotic resistance genes flanked by the gene mobility elements tnpA-sul1 (pNAR1ΔblaDHA-1)
evidence: Identified through whole genome sequencing of evolved lineages

claim: One FK688 lineage lost the entire pNAR1 plasmid.
source: while the second lineage lost the entire pNAR1 plasmid (pNAR1‾; Figure 3B, Figure 3C).
evidence: Identified through whole genome sequencing of evolved lineages

claim: Loss of pNAR1, and specifically the tnpA-sul1 region of pNAR1, caused a loss of resistance to ceftazidime and carbapenem.
source: We assayed both the pNAR1‾ and pNAR1ΔblaDHA-1 strains for growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—source data 1) and antibiotic sensitivity (Table 2) and confirmed that loss of pNAR1, and specifically the tnpA-sul1 region of pNAR1, caused a loss of resistance to ceftazidime and carbapenem.
evidence: Confirmed through growth assays and MIC testing

claim: The acquisition of carbapenem-resistance in FK688 required the combination of the absence of porins and the β-lactamase DHA-1.
source: The results demonstrate that the acquisition of carbapenem-resistance in FK688 required the combination of (i) the absence of porins and (ii) the β-lactamase DHA-1 (Figure 1—source data 6).
evidence: Demonstrated through genetic reconstruction and MIC testing of all genotype combinations

claim: The blaDHA-1 and ΔompK36 alleles conferred a substantial fitness cost in growth media without antibiotic compared to other strains tested.
source: We found that the blaDHA-1 and ΔompK36 alleles conferred a substantial fitness cost in growth media without antibiotic as compared to the other strains tested (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Measured through competitive fitness assays

claim: The fitness defects of blaDHA-1 and ΔompK36 alleles in the absence of imipenem are gradually reversed in strains grown in the presence of increasing concentrations of imipenem.
source: These assays showed that the fitness defects seen in the absence of imipenem (Figure 4B) are gradually reversed in the strains grown in the presence of increasing concentrations imipenem (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through fitness assays across imipenem concentration gradients

claim: At the imipenem breakpoint value of 0.125 µg/mL, three genotypes (ompK36+pNAR1ΔblaDHA-1, ompK36+pNAR1, and ΔompK36 pNAR1‾) are at a selective disadvantage.
source: At the breakpoint value of 0.125 µg/mL, three genotypes are already at a selective disadvantage: ompK36+pNAR1ΔblaDHA-1, ompK36+pNAR1, and ΔompK36 pNAR1‾.
evidence: Measured through competitive fitness assays at specific imipenem concentrations

claim: Above the imipenem breakpoint value at 0.25 µg/mL, all four genotypes are at a selective disadvantage relative to the parental FK688.
source: Above the breakpoint value at 0.25 µg/mL, all four genotypes are at a selective disadvantage relative to the parental FK688.
evidence: Measured through competitive fitness assays at specific imipenem concentrations

claim: A clinically relevant appearance of the CRE phenotype requires a combination of the presence of DHA-1 and the lack of a functional porin.
source: Thus, a clinically relevant appearance of the CRE phenotype requires a combination of the presence of DHA-1 and the lack of a functional porin.
evidence: Concluded from fitness assays across imipenem concentrations and MIC data

claim: The ΔompK36 pNAR1 (lineage A) populations evolved similar competitive fitness to the ompK36+ pNAR1 (lineage B) evolved populations, recovering the fitness cost of the ΔompK36 mutation.
source: The ΔompK36 pNAR1 (lineage A) populations evolved similar competitive fitness to the ompK36+ pNAR1 (lineage B) evolved populations, recovering the fitness cost of the ΔompK36 mutation (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Measured through competitive fitness assays after 200 generations of evolution

claim: Four evolved strains (A2(o), A2(t), B3(o), and B3(t)) each independently sustained a deletion in pNAR1 that removed blaDHA-1.
source: To understand the molecular basis of these phenotypes, whole genome sequence data was analysed for four evolved strains: A2(o), A2(t), B3(o), and B3(t). Each, independently, sustained a deletion in pNAR1 that removed blaDHA-1.
evidence: Identified through whole genome sequencing of evolved strains

claim: The deletion of blaDHA-1 explains the increased carbapenem sensitivity of the ΔompK36 pNAR1 and ompK36+ pNAR1 lineages.
source: This explains the increased carbapenem sensitivity of the ΔompK36 pNAR1 and ompK36+ pNAR1 lineages as they had now lost one of the genes contributing to provide the phenotype.
evidence: Inferred from genetic reconstruction experiments showing both genes are required

claim: After 200 generations of evolution, samples displayed a mixture of opaque and translucent colony morphotypes.
source: After 200 generations of evolution, samples were plated on agar and were found to display a mixture of opaque and translucent colony morphotypes from each strain (Figure 5B and Figure 5D).
evidence: Observed through colony morphology analysis

claim: The opaque/translucent colony morphotype feature depends on the expression of type 1 fimbriae.
source: This feature has been seen before in Klebsiella spp. and depends on the expression of type 1 fimbriae (Matatov et al., 1999; Klemm, 1986; Struve et al., 2008).
evidence: Established from cited literature on Klebsiella colony morphology

claim: In the B3(o) isolate, a transposase gene (IS4 family) insertion disrupted the downstream region of the fimE gene.
source: In the single B3(o) isolate recovered, a transposase gene (IS4 family) insertion had disrupted the downstream region of the fimE gene (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: Identified through whole genome sequencing

claim: The fimE gene was not disrupted in the A2 population that was capable of phase-switching.
source: The fimE gene was not disrupted in the A2 population that was capable of phase-switching (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Identified through whole genome sequencing

claim: The A2(o) and B3(o) strains had more capsular polysaccharide than A2(t) and B3(t) strains.
source: Consistent with these observations, an assay measuring glucuronic acid that reflects the presence of capsule showed that the A2(o) and B3(o) had more capsular polysaccharide than A2(t) and B3(t) (Figure 5E, Figure 5—source data 4).
evidence: Measured through glucuronic acid colorimetric assay

claim: The lineage A evolved strains (A2(o) and A2(t)) showed 64-fold increased sensitivity to imipenem compared to the ancestor.
source: MIC analysis of the lineage A evolved strains showed that the ΔompK36 pNAR1 populations had evolved increased sensitivity to imipenem, 64-fold for the A2(o) and A2(t) strains, bringing them to the same MIC value as the B3(t) strain (Table 3).
evidence: Measured through MIC assays

claim: The primary determinant of the reversion of the AMR phenotype in evolved strains is the observed loss of the blaDHA-1 gene from the megaplasmid pNAR1.
source: Our reconstruction experiments (Table 2) suggest that the primary determinant of this reversion of the AMR phenotype is the observed loss of the blaDHA-1 gene from the megaplasmid pNAR1.
evidence: Inferred from genetic reconstruction experiments showing requirement of blaDHA-1 for resistance

claim: The blaDHA-1 gene was selectively favoured even at concentrations of ceftazidime approximately 100× below the clinical breakpoint of 16 µg/mL.
source: This showed that blaDHA-1 was selectively favoured, even at concentrations of ceftazidime approximately 100× below the clinical breakpoint of 16 µg/mL, despite the fact that carriage of the blaDHA-1 gene bears a substantial fitness cost (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated through fitness assays across ceftazidime concentration gradients

claim: The OmpK36 inactivating mutation reduced fitness in ceftazidime.
source: In addition, we found that the OmpK36 inactivating mutation reduced fitness in ceftazidime
evidence: Measured through fitness assays in ceftazidime

claim: Selection on ceftazidime can select for the blaDHA-1 gene, but not for the ompK36 mutation, which is required for imipenem resistance.
source: confirming that selection on ceftazidime can select for the blaDHA-1 gene, but not for the ompK36 mutation, which is required for imipenem resistance.
evidence: Concluded from fitness assays showing differential selection effects

claim: Strains that carried only the ΔompK36 allele, or neither allele, were unable to evolve imipenem resistance.
source: We found that strains that carried only the ΔompK36 allele, or neither allele, were unable to evolve imipenem resistance (Figure 6B; "A" and "C").
evidence: Demonstrated by plating 10^9 cells on imipenem and observing no resistant colonies

claim: A K. quasipneumoniae strain with the pNAR1 plasmid (carrying the blaDHA-1 gene) would be readily able to evolve imipenem resistance.
source: However, a K. quasipneumoniae strain with the pNAR1 plasmid (carrying the blaDHA-1 gene) would be readily able to evolve imipenem resistance (Figure 6B; "B").
evidence: Demonstrated by plating 10^9 cells on imipenem and observing resistant colonies

claim: The most likely evolutionary path to imipenem resistance in FK688 was A → B → D (no resistance alleles → blaDHA-1 → blaDHA-1 + ΔompK36).
source: Thus, in a scenario representing previous treatment of a patient with ceftazidime, given the low fitness benefit conferred by the loss of function mutation in ompK36 in growth media supplemented with imipenem, the path A → B → D is most likely.
evidence: Inferred from fitness data and evolutionary potential experiments

claim: This study presented the first physical genetic map of a K. quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae genome.
source: This study presented the first physical genetic map of a K. quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae genome.
evidence: Stated as a novel contribution of the study

claim: Carbapenem sensitivity was readily restored in FK688 in the absence of drug selection.
source: A major finding of the study is the ease with which carbapenem sensitivity was restored in the absence of drug selection.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental evolution showing loss of resistance genes

claim: An ill-chosen drug treatment with ceftazidime can prime a population of K. quasipneumoniae to rapidly evolve a CRE phenotype.
source: A further major finding is the means by which an ill-chosen drug treatment, for example with ceftazidime, can prime a population of K. quasipneumoniae to rapidly evolve a CRE phenotype.
evidence: Demonstrated through fitness assays showing ceftazidime selects for blaDHA-1

claim: KPC-2 carbapenemases are widespread in Klebsiella spp. including K. quasipneumoniae.
source: Genomics-based surveillance has shown that KPC-2 carbapenemases are widespread in Klebsiella spp. including K. quasipneumoniae (Mathers et al., 2019; Octavia et al., 2019).
evidence: Established from cited surveillance studies

claim: blaSHV is found in K. pneumoniae, blaOKP-A in K. quasipneumoniae subsp. quasipneumoniae and blaOKP-B in K. quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae.
source: β-lactamases encoded by chromosomal genes are common amongst these species of Klebsiella: blaSHV is found in K. pneumoniae, blaOKP-A in K. quasipneumoniae subsp. quasipneumoniae and blaOKP-B in K. quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae (Rodrigues et al., 2019; Long et al., 2017; Fevre et al., 2005).
evidence: Established from cited literature

claim: FK688 carries a chromosomally located blaOKP-B gene.
source: Consistent with this, FK688 carries a chromosomally located blaOKP-B.
evidence: Identified through genome annotation

claim: FK688 carries the β-lactamase blaDHA-1 on the megaplasmid pNAR1.
source: In addition, FK688 also carries the β-lactamase blaDHA-1 on the megaplasmid pNAR1.
evidence: Identified through genome annotation

claim: In FK688, efflux pumps did not contribute to carbapenem resistance.
source: In FK688, the efflux pumps did not contribute to carbapenem resistance.
evidence: Concluded from genetic reconstruction experiments showing only blaDHA-1 and ΔompK36 are required

claim: The CRE phenotype in FK688 depends on epistasis between blaDHA-1 and ompK36.
source: Instead, we found that the CRE phenotype in FK688 depends on epistasis between blaDHA-1 and ompK36.
evidence: Demonstrated through genetic reconstruction showing both are required and have non-additive fitness effects

claim: Both the carriage of blaDHA-1 and the defect in ompK36 have measurable fitness cost to the strain.
source: Both the carriage of blaDHA-1 and the defect in ompK36 have measurable fitness cost to the strain.
evidence: Measured through competitive fitness assays

claim: The presence of plasmids encoding DHA-1 is geographically wide-spread.
source: (i) the presence of plasmids encoding DHA-1 is geographically wide-spread (Hennequin et al., 2012)
evidence: Established from cited literature

claim: The presence of ompK35 and/or ompK36 mutations is prevalent in the various species of Klebsiella.
source: (ii) the presence of ompK35 and/or ompK36 mutations is prevalent in the various species of Klebsiella (Rocker et al., 2020)
evidence: Established from cited literature

claim: A recent case study showed a single hospital had collected 87 isolates of CRE Klebsiella with 55% of them being a non-carbapenemase CRE phenotype.
source: a recent case study showed a single hospital had collected 87 isolates of CRE Klebsiella with 55% of them being a non-carbapenemase CRE phenotype (Tamma et al., 2017a).
evidence: Reported from cited case study

claim: All currently available tests for CRE aim to identify specific carbapenemases.
source: All of the currently available tests for CRE aim to identify specific carbapenemases: the Carba NP test detects OXA-48 type carbapenemases, the modified Hodge test identifies metallo-β-lactamases (Kuchibiro et al., 2018), and the newer more sophisticated gene-specific tests also have limitations (Tamma et al., 2017b; Powell et al., 2017; Revez et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2019; Meunier et al., 2018).
evidence: Established from cited literature on diagnostic methods

claim: In some environments perhaps half of all CRE cases could be caused by strains that do not encode a carbapenemase.
source: The finding that in some environments perhaps half of all CRE cases could be caused by strains that do not encode a carbapenemase (Tamma et al., 2017a)
evidence: Reported from cited study

claim: Combination therapy using an ESBL inhibitor such as avibactam or tazobactam could be a good option for non-carbapenemase CRE.
source: combination therapy using an ESBL inhibitor such as avibactam or tazobactam could be a good option for this type of CRE (Yahav et al., 2020).
evidence: Proposed based on mechanism of resistance and supported by citation

claim: Ceftolozane-tazobactam combination therapy is suggested as an alternative to carbapenems in treatment of some CRE infections.
source: For example, the use of ceftolozane-tazobactam combination therapy is suggested as an alternative to carbapenems in treatment of some CRE infections (Giacobbe et al., 2018)
evidence: Established from cited literature

claim: A cohort study of 391 patients with ceftriaxone-resistant infections showed piperacillin-tazobactam combination therapy compared favourably with carbapenem treatment.
source: and a cohort study of 391 patients with ceftriaxone-resistant infections showed piperacillin-tazobactam combination therapy compared favourably with carbapenem treatment (Harris et al., 2018).
evidence: Reported from cited clinical study

claim: In strains like FK688 where a β-lactamase such as DHA-1 contributes to carbapenem resistance, specific inhibition of that β-lactamase with avibactam or tazobactam would increase the effectiveness of drug treatment.
source: In strains like FK688, where it is a β-lactamase such as DHA-1 that contributes to carbapenem resistance, specific inhibition of that β-lactamase with avibactam or tazobactam would increase the level of carbapenem or cephalosporin in the bacterial periplasm and thereby increase the effectiveness of drug treatment.
evidence: Inferred from mechanism of resistance and known action of β-lactamase inhibitors

claim: Phage therapy for CRE should avoid the use of phages that use OmpK35 or OmpK36 as their receptor.
source: Second, our study cautions that moves towards phage therapy being used to treat CRE should avoid the use of phages that use OmpK35 or OmpK36 as their receptor (Rosas and Lithgow, 2022).
evidence: Recommended based on findings and supported by citation

claim: Phages that use OmpK35 or OmpK36 as their receptor would place selective pressure on Klebsiella to become porin-defective since mutations to inactivate the receptor is a prime cause of phage-resistance.
source: These phages would place selective pressure on the Klebsiella strain to become porin-defective since mutations to inactivate the receptor is a prime cause of phage-resistance (Gordillo Altamirano et al., 2021; Gordillo Altamirano and Barr, 2021).
evidence: Inferred from known mechanisms of phage resistance supported by citations

claim: Phages that use OmpK35 or OmpK36 as their receptor would inadvertently select for carbapenem-resistance.
source: Phages that use OmpK35 or OmpK36 as their receptor would thereby select for porin-defects and thus inadvertently select for carbapenem-resistance
evidence: Inferred from findings showing porin defects contribute to carbapenem resistance

claim: The evolutionary history of a pathogenic strain can predispose for an AMR phenotype to evolve via specific genetic routes.
source: Finally, this study shows how the evolutionary history of a pathogenic strain can predispose for an AMR phenotype to evolve via specific genetic routes.
evidence: Concluded from experimental evolution and fitness data showing sequential selection

claim: If antibiotic resistance genes confer a decrease in fitness in environments without antibiotic, then these variants will be exceedingly rare or absent from the population.
source: If the genes or genetic variants that confer resistance to the antibiotic confer a decrease in fitness in environments without antibiotic, then these variants will be exceedingly rare (or absent) from the population.
evidence: Based on established evolutionary principles

claim: The spontaneous acquisition of multiple genetic variants (ΔompK36 and blaDHA-1) is much less likely than the acquisition of a single new gene (KPC-2 carbapenemase).
source: Since the spontaneous acquisition of multiple genetic variants (for example,ΔompK36 and blaDHA-1) is much less likely than the acquisition of a single new gene (KPC-2 carbapenemase), the evolution of non-carbapenem resistance via two loci seemed unlikely.
evidence: Based on probability of multiple independent mutations versus horizontal gene transfer

claim: If a strain already carries the blaDHA-1 gene then the spontaneous evolution of a loss-of-function mutation in ompK36 is more likely than the spontaneous acquisition of a carbapenemase gene.
source: However, if a strain already carries the blaDHA-1 gene then the spontaneous evolution of a loss-of-function mutation in an extant chromosomal gene - ompK36 - is more likely than the spontaneous acquisition of a carbapenemase gene.
evidence: Based on probability of single mutation versus horizontal gene transfer

claim: Exposure to ceftazidime, or any antibiotic that selects for the blaDHA-1 gene, would potentiate the evolution of carbapenem resistance by a single loss-of-function mutation in major porins.
source: Exposure to ceftazidime, or any antibiotic that selects for the blaDHA-1 gene, would therefore potentiate the evolution of carbapenem resistance by a single loss-of-function mutation in major porins.
evidence: Concluded from fitness data showing ceftazidime selects for blaDHA-1

claim: An individual's treatment history might shape the evolution of AMR and should be taken into consideration to explain the evolution of non-carbapenemase CRE.
source: These results show how an individual's treatment history might shape the evolution of AMR and should be taken into consideration in order to explain the evolution of non-carbapenemase CRE.
evidence: Concluded from experimental data showing sequential selection pathway

claim: Carbapenems are a class of β-lactam antibiotics typically reserved for high-risk, multidrug-resistant infections.
source: Carbapenems are a class of β-lactam antibiotics typically reserved for high-risk, multidrug-resistant infections (Doi, 2019; Meletis, 2016).
evidence: Established clinical knowledge supported by citations

claim: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE), especially various species of Klebsiella, have become a widespread problem in clinical settings around the globe.
source: Surveillance studies show that carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE), especially various species of the pathogen Klebsiella, have become a widespread problem in clinical settings around the globe (Hansen, 2021; Hu et al., 2016; Logan and Weinstein, 2017).
evidence: Reported from cited surveillance studies

claim: There are two general mechanisms of carbapenem resistance: acquisition of a carbapenemase gene, or multiple genetic loci including overexpressed β-lactamase and/or efflux pump and/or inactivated outer membrane protein.
source: There are two general mechanisms of carbapenem resistance. The first and readily diagnosable mechanism is the acquisition of a single gene encoding a carbapenemase enzyme that directly inactivates the antibiotic. The second mechanism requires multiple genetic loci, and bacterial strains in this category often have an over expressed β-lactamase and/or an overexpressed efflux pump and/or an inactivated outer membrane protein (Meletis, 2016; Codjoe and Donkor, 2017; Elshamy and Aboshanab, 2020)
evidence: Established from cited literature

claim: Most carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae identified so far are caused by carbapenemases.
source: Of these two mechanisms, most carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae that have been identified so far are caused by carbapenemases.
evidence: General statement about prevalence in literature

claim: There are two structurally distinct classes of carbapenemases: metallo-β-lactamases and serine-based carbapenemases.
source: Like other β-lactamases, carbapenemases can be recognised by sequence analysis (Wang et al., 2021), and there are two structurally distinct classes of carbapenemases: the first is the metallo-β-lactamases a family of enzymes that contains a metal ion (usually zinc) coordinated in the active site, a classic example of which is NDM-1 (Khan et al., 2017). The second carbapenemase family does not coordinate a metal ion but instead relies on an active site serine to hydrolyse carbapenem drugs (Codjoe and Donkor, 2017; Nordmann and Poirel, 2019).
evidence: Established biochemical knowledge supported by citations

claim: The KPC enzymes are archetypal K. pneumoniae carbapenemases.
source: This second class of carbapenemase includes the IMI, OXA-48, and GES enzymes in addition to the archetypal K. pneumoniae carbapenemases: the KPC enzymes (Nordmann and Poirel, 2019; Rapp and Urban, 2012; Yigit et al., 2001)
evidence: Established from cited literature

claim: The KPC-2 carbapenemase has become widespread and is found in many clinical investigations of CRE.
source: The KPC-2 carbapenemase has become widespread, found in many clinical investigations of CRE
evidence: General statement about prevalence

claim: The gene encoding KPC-2 carbapenemase (blaKPC-2) is transferred readily by horizontal gene transfer via plasmids.
source: and the gene encoding this enzyme - blaKPC-2 - is transferred readily by horizontal gene transfer via plasmids (Bowers et al., 2015; Hardiman et al., 2016; Kitchel et al., 2009; Petrella et al., 2008; Wyres et al., 2019).
evidence: Established from cited literature

claim: Carbapenem resistance caused by the presence of a carbapenemase is readily diagnosed by whole genome sequencing or simple PCR-based genome tests.
source: Since this is a monogenic phenotype, carbapenem resistance caused by the presence of a carbapenemase is readily diagnosed by whole genome sequencing or even simple PCR-based genome tests.
evidence: Based on established diagnostic methods

claim: Numerous CRE infections do not depend on the expression of carbapenemases.
source: It has recently become apparent that numerous CRE infections do not depend on the expression of carbapenemases
evidence: Emerging recognition in the field

claim: There is mounting evidence that non-carbapenemase CRE are widespread.
source: and there is mounting evidence that these non-carbapenemase CRE are widespread (Bouganim et al., 2020).
evidence: Reported from cited literature

claim: Non-carbapenemase CRE emerge because of reduced outer membrane permeability and/or increased drug efflux.
source: Based on the limited cases identified for non-carbapenemase CRE so far, it has been suggested that they emerge because of reduced outer membrane permeability and/or increased drug efflux (Logan and Weinstein, 2017; Goodman et al., 2016; Tamma et al., 2017a).
evidence: Suggested mechanism from cited literature

claim: In some genetic backgrounds, an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) could provide sufficient activity against carbapenems to generate a CRE phenotype.
source: Other studies have suggested that, at least in some genetic backgrounds, an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) could provide sufficient activity against carbapenems as to generate a CRE phenotype (Codjoe and Donkor, 2017; Halat et al., 2016).
evidence: Suggested from cited studies

claim: Few studies have directly demonstrated the cause of non-carbapenemase CRE.
source: Despite this emerging knowledge, few studies have directly demonstrated the cause of non-carbapenemase CRE
evidence: Assessment of current literature

claim: The evolutionary forces that shape the evolution of non-carbapenemase CRE have not been addressed.
source: and the evolutionary forces that shape the evolution of this trait have not been addressed.
evidence: Assessment of gap in current literature

claim: A patient died as a result of septicaemia caused by Klebsiella isolate FK688, where the infection did not respond to treatment with carbapenems.
source: A patient died as a result of septicaemia caused by a Klebsiella isolate, FK688, where the infection did not respond to treatment with carbapenems (Bi et al., 2017).
evidence: Clinical case reported in cited literature

claim: Non-carbapenemase CRE strains are unfit and readily evolve to be drug-sensitive in the absence of carbapenem antibiotics.
source: We show that non-carbapenemase CRE strains are unfit and readily evolve to be drug-sensitive in the absence of carbapenem antibiotics.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental evolution experiments

claim: The evolution of non-carbapenemase CRE strains may be contingent on their recent exposure to antibiotics that select for other β-lactamases.
source: The evolution of these low-fitness CRE strains may be contingent on their recent exposure to antibiotics that select for other β-lactamases which may explain the evolution of non-carbepenemase CRE.
evidence: Inferred from fitness assays showing ceftazidime selects for blaDHA-1

claim: Porins are β-barrel proteins that transport nutrients across the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria but can also admit antibiotics into the bacterial cell.
source: Porins are β-barrel proteins that transport nutrients across the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria but can also admit antibiotics into the bacterial cell (Martínez-Martínez et al., 1996; Nicolas-Chanoine et al., 2018; Rocker et al., 2020).
evidence: Established biochemical knowledge supported by citations

claim: The ancestral FK688 strains (ΔompK36 pNAR1 and ompK36+ pNAR1) have an opaque colony morphology.
source: The ancestral FK688 strains (ΔompK36 pNAR1 and ompK36+ pNAR1) have an opaque colony morphology.
evidence: Observed colony morphology

claim: Opaque colony morphology in Klebsiella is consistent with capsular polysaccharide production in non-fimbriated strains.
source: This is consistent with a phenotype of capsular polysaccharide production: non-fimbriated Klebsiella strains are mucoid due to capsule secretion and look opaque, while translucent colonies are fimbriated and non-mucoid (Matatov et al., 1999; Schembri et al., 2005; Wilksch et al., 2011).
evidence: Established from cited literature on Klebsiella phenotypes

claim: The replicate population ompK36+ pNAR1 (B3) was almost entirely (594 of 595 colonies observed) made up of translucent colony-forming cells after 200 generations.
source: while for the replicate population ompK36+ pNAR1 (B3) was almost entirely (594 of 595 colonies observed) made up of translucent colony-forming cells
evidence: Counted colony morphotypes
